4076784.note: Alabama's capital since 1846, it was the first capital of the Confederacy — and a century later, the endpoint of the Selma to Montgomery marches. Rosa Parks' 1955 bus boycott began on its streets.

4119403.note: Central High School here was the 1957 desegregation battleground, where the Little Rock Nine braved mobs under federal guard.

4142290.note: Delaware was the first state to ratify the Constitution — hence 'the First State.' Dover has been its capital since 1777.

4174715.note: Chosen as capital in 1824 as the midpoint between St. Augustine and Pensacola. Its name is Muskogean for 'old town.'

4180439.note: Burned by Sherman in 1864, it rose to host the 1996 Olympics. Martin Luther King Jr. was born here.

4250542.note: Lincoln lived here 24 years before the presidency, and his tomb still draws pilgrims from around the world.

4259418.note: The Indy 500 has run at the Brickyard since 1911. The Soldiers and Sailors Monument anchors the city's center.

4280539.note: Brown v. Board of Education began here — the 1954 ruling that ended school segregation nationwide.

4292188.note: Named for pioneer Stephen Frank, killed at the river ford in 1780. Daniel Boone is buried in its cemetery.

4315588.note: French for 'red stick,' a boundary marker seen by explorers in 1699. Its 34-story Capitol is the tallest state capitol in America.

4347242.note: The U.S. Naval Academy has trained officers here since 1845. Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris in its State House.

4392388.note: Named for Thomas Jefferson while he was still alive. Its 1836–2004 state penitentiary was the oldest operating prison west of the Mississippi — 'the bloodiest 47 acres in America.'

4431410.note: Named for Andrew Jackson and burned three times in the Civil War — Sherman's men called it 'Chimneyville.'

4487042.note: Named for Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of the Lost Colony. It anchors the Research Triangle.

4509177.note: Named for Christopher Columbus and now America's 14th-largest city. Ohio State's campus fuels its growth.

4544349.note: Born in a single day — the 1889 Land Run staked thousands of claims by sunset. Its memorial honors the 1995 bombing victims.

4575352.note: Sherman's troops burned it in 1865 — who started the fire is still debated. The University of South Carolina was founded here in 1801.

4644585.note: Music City — the Grand Ole Opry has broadcast here since 1925. Its full-scale Parthenon replica earned it 'Athens of the South.'

4671654.note: Named for Stephen F. Austin, 'Father of Texas.' 'Keep Austin Weird' and its live-music scene define it.

4781708.note: Capital of the Confederacy; its fall in 1865 ended the Civil War. Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty' speech rang out here.

4801859.note: Named for early settler Charles Clendenin. Its gold-leaf Capitol dome gleams over the Kanawha River.

4835797.note: Mark Twain wrote his most famous books in his Hartford home, now a museum. Insurance wealth once made it one of America's richest cities.

4853828.note: Its name is French for 'of the monks.' Every four years the Iowa caucuses put it at the center of presidential politics.

4930956.note: The Freedom Trail walks the Revolution: the Tea Party, Paul Revere's ride, Bunker Hill. Harvard, founded 1636, is across the river.

4957003.note: Named for the daughter of Revolutionary War general Henry Dearborn. It is one of America's smallest capitals.

4998830.note: Made capital in 1847 to move government inland from border-town Detroit. It is named for Lansing, New York, an early settler's hometown.

5045360.note: The head of Mississippi River navigation made it a fur-trade hub. F. Scott Fitzgerald was born here.

5072006.note: Renamed for Abraham Lincoln after his assassination — the first city to bear his name. Its 400-foot Capitol tower is a landmark for miles.

5084868.note: Named for harmony after a boundary dispute was settled. Christa McAuliffe taught here before the Challenger mission.

5105496.note: Washington's Christmas-night crossing and the 1776 Battle of Trenton turned the Revolution's tide.

5106834.note: Chartered in 1686, among America's oldest cities. The Erie Canal made it a 19th-century boomtown.

5192726.note: A key Underground Railroad crossing on the Susquehanna. Three Mile Island's 1979 accident happened just downstream.

5224151.note: Founded 1636 by Roger Williams as a haven for religious freedom. Brown University has stood on College Hill since 1764.

5238685.note: America's smallest capital, under 8,000 people. Named for Montpellier, France.

5261457.note: Built on an isthmus between two lakes and named for James Madison. Its Capitol dome is the largest granite dome in the world.

5308655.note: America's hottest major city, built over ancient Hohokam canals. It is now the fifth-largest city in the United States.

5389489.note: Born in the Gold Rush and capital since 1854. The western end of the Transcontinental Railroad was built here.

5419384.note: The Mile High City — a medallion on the Capitol steps marks exactly 5,280 feet. It boomed on Pikes Peak gold.

5490263.note: America's oldest capital city, founded in 1610 — a decade before the Pilgrims landed. Its adobe Plaza still anchors downtown.

5501344.note: Named for Kit Carson and built on Comstock Lode silver. Its U.S. Mint stamped the coveted 'CC' coins.

5554072.note: Alaska's capital is unreachable by road — you can only arrive by boat or plane. It was named for Joe Juneau, a gold prospector who struck it rich here in 1880.

5586437.note: French-Canadian trappers named it crying 'les bois!' — 'the woods!' It is pronounced BOY-see, never boy-ZEE.

5656882.note: Born as 'Last Chance Gulch' in the 1864 gold rush. Its grand Capitol rose on copper-boom money.

5688025.note: Named for Germany's Otto von Bismarck to lure railroad investment. Its 19-story Capitol is the 'Skyscraper on the Prairie.'

5750162.note: Named for the Hebrew word for peace. It grew rich on Willamette Valley hops and cherries.

5767918.note: One of America's smallest capitals, on the Missouri River. It took the title at statehood in 1889.

5780993.note: Founded 1847 by Brigham Young and Mormon pioneers. Temple Square anchors its downtown.

5805687.note: Named for the Olympic Mountains across Puget Sound. Its downtown artesian well still flows with free spring water.

5821086.note: Named for the Cheyenne Nation and raised on railroad money. Frontier Days, running since 1897, is billed as the world's largest rodeo.

5856195.note: The only U.S. state capital with a royal palace — ʻIolani Palace housed Hawaii's last monarchs. Pearl Harbor lies just west.

_comment: Curated memorable facts for notable GeoNames places, keyed by geonameid. Merged into blurbs at dataset build time (scripts/build-geonames-dataset.mjs). Every note is a verifiable fact in the starters' voice: 1-2 sentences, evocative, no filler. wiki is the en.wikipedia.org article slug for attribution.
